specPoints.text: understand how to name compounds relevant to this specification using the rules of International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature students will be expected to name compounds containing up to six carbon atoms

primer.text: From Organic Compounds you already know that molecules are drawn five ways and that families share a functional group. This note turns drawings into names: the two-part naming system, the number prefixes that count carbon atoms, and the position numbers that say exactly where the reactive part sits.

lessons.title: The two-part name: stem and suffix
lessons.opening: Every organic name in this course splits into two useful halves. The first half counts the carbon atoms in the longest chain, and the second half names the functional group carried by that chain.
keyPoints: An organic name splits into the stem or prefix, which counts the carbon atoms, and the suffix.
The stem counts the carbon atoms: meth is 1, eth is 2, prop is 3, but is 4, pent is 5 and hex is 6.
The suffix names the functional group: ane for none, ene for a C=C bond, anol for an OH group.
So methanol is a 1-carbon molecule carrying the alcohol group, and butene has 4 carbons with a double bond.
The rules come from IUPAC, and compounds with up to six carbon atoms are expected in exams.

low.restatement: Names are built in two blocks: the stem counts carbons and the suffix gives the reactive group. Meth means one carbon, eth two, prop three, but four, pent five and hex six.
low.analogy: It works like a vehicle badge: the first word tells you the engine size and the second tells you the body style, so a name like propene reads as three carbons wearing a double bond.
low.examPointer: Learn the six stems as a chant; every naming question starts by counting the longest chain.

medium.restatement: IUPAC names combine a stem, which records how many carbon atoms sit in the longest continuous chain, with a suffix, which records the functional group present. The suffixes ane, ene and anol flag no special group, a C=C double bond and an alcohol group respectively, up to hex for six carbons.
medium.analogy: Think of the name as a postcode: the stem is the street of carbons and the suffix is the house number of reactivity, and together they locate the molecule unambiguously.
medium.examPointer: Count the longest continuous chain before choosing a stem, and check the suffix against the functional group you can actually see drawn.

check.stem: How many carbon atoms does the stem pent stand for?

options.explanation: Pent is the fifth stem: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5.
Four carbons is the stem but, one step below pent.
Six carbons is hex, the stem above pent.
Three carbons is prop, which shares no letters with pent worth trusting.

check.stem: What information does the suffix of an organic name carry?

options.text: Which functional group the compound carries
options.explanation: The end part of the name names the reactive group, such as ene for a C=C bond.

options.text: How many carbon atoms are in the chain
options.explanation: Carbon counting belongs to the stem at the front of the name.

options.text: The boiling point of the compound
options.explanation: Physical data never appears in the name; the suffix is structural information.

options.text: The state of the compound at room temperature
options.explanation: State is a physical property; the suffix records the functional group instead.

check.stem: Which name matches a 2-carbon molecule with a C=C double bond?

options.text: Ethene
options.explanation: Eth gives two carbons and ene gives the double bond, so the assembly is ethene.

options.text: Methene
options.explanation: One carbon cannot carry a C=C bond, and meth is the wrong stem for two carbons.

options.text: Ethane
options.explanation: The suffix ane means no special group; the double bond demands ene.

options.text: Ethanediol
options.explanation: That name points to an alcohol-family compound, not a 2-carbon alkene.

check.stem: A molecule named butanol contains how many carbon atoms, and which family?

options.text: 4 carbon atoms, the alcohol family
options.explanation: The stem but counts four carbons and the suffix anol places it in the alcohol family.

options.text: 4 carbon atoms, the alkene family
options.explanation: Alkenes carry the suffix ene; anol signals the alcohol group instead.

options.text: 3 carbon atoms, the alcohol family
options.explanation: Three carbons would be propanol; but always means four.

options.text: 5 carbon atoms, the alkane family
options.explanation: Five carbons is pent, and alkanes end in ane, neither of which matches butanol.

check.stem: Why do IUPAC rules matter for naming compounds?

options.text: They give every compound one unambiguous name scientists worldwide can use
options.explanation: A shared rulebook means a name reconstructs the same structure in any laboratory.

options.text: They shorten all names to three letters
options.explanation: The rules aim for precision, not brevity; names grow longer as structures grow richer.

options.text: They let chemists rename compounds daily
options.explanation: The opposite is true: fixed rules keep names stable over time.

options.text: They only apply to compounds with six or more carbons
options.explanation: The rules apply throughout; six carbons is just the exam expectation ceiling.

lessons.title: Position numbers and naming isomers
lessons.opening: When a chain grows longer, the functional group could sit in several places, so the name needs an address. This lesson adds the numbering rules, the di- prefix, and how the same rules separate isomers.
keyPoints: Carbon atoms in the chain are numbered so the name can say exactly which carbon carries the functional group.
Numbering distinguishes positions when a functional group could sit on more than one carbon atom.
The prefix di- is attached to the second part of the name when two identical functional groups are present.
Isomers are told apart by applying the same naming rules to their different structures.
For this course you mainly name straight-chain compounds and unbranched isomers, with numbers read as side-chain positions.

low.restatement: Longer chains need addresses: the carbons are numbered, and the name quotes the number where the functional group sits. Two identical groups earn the prefix di-. The same rules applied carefully give isomers their separate, correct names.
low.analogy: It is like flats in a block: the stem names the building, the number picks the floor, and di- says you occupy two floors at once.
low.examPointer: Use the position number whenever the group could sit elsewhere; a bare name is only unambiguous for the shortest chains.

medium.restatement: When a functional group could attach to more than one carbon, each carbon is numbered and the numbers are written into the name to locate the group exactly. Two identical groups take the prefix di- before the second part of the name, and the same rules distinguish isomers by describing their different arrangements.
medium.analogy: A street with identical houses needs house numbers to deliver post correctly; numbering carbons plays that role, and di- is the note that says two deliveries at the same address type.
medium.examPointer: Expect to name unbranched chains fluently and to interpret branched numbers even if you need not invent branched names yourself.

check.stem: Why are the carbon atoms in a chain numbered when naming?

options.text: To record exactly which carbon carries the functional group
options.explanation: The number in the name is the address of the reactive group on the chain.

options.text: To count the total number of atoms in the molecule
options.explanation: Total counting is the stem job; numbering is about position along the chain.

options.text: To show the order in which the atoms were discovered
options.explanation: Discovery order never enters the naming system.

options.text: To rank the atoms by reactivity
options.explanation: Numbering locates groups; it does not rank them.

check.stem: A molecule carries two identical functional groups. How is its name adjusted?

options.text: The prefix di- is added to the second part of the name
options.explanation: Two identical groups are flagged with di- before the suffix part of the name.

options.text: The suffix is deleted because groups cancel out
options.explanation: Groups never cancel; both must be reflected in the name.

options.text: The stem is doubled instead of the suffix
options.explanation: The doubling convention attaches to the second part of the name, not the stem.

options.text: The name is left unchanged because groups share one position
options.explanation: Two groups need two positions recorded; silence would misdescribe the molecule.

check.stem: How does the naming system cope with isomers?

options.text: The same rules applied to each structure produce different, correct names
options.explanation: Because the rules encode chain length and group position, each arrangement earns its own name.

options.text: Isomers all share one name because their formula matches
options.explanation: A shared molecular formula does not force a shared name; arrangement changes the name.

options.text: Isomers are named by adding numbers chosen at random
options.explanation: Position numbers follow fixed rules about where the group sits, never randomness.

options.text: Isomers cannot be named, so they are labelled A and B
options.explanation: The naming system handles isomers precisely; letter labels are not part of it.

check.stem: What do the numbers in a branched name such as 2-methylbutane tell you?

options.text: Where the side chain sits relative to the main chain
options.explanation: The number fixes the position of the side chain along the main chain.

options.text: How many side chains the molecule has
options.explanation: Counting side chains is a separate job; the number locates a side chain.

options.text: The temperature at which the compound boils
options.explanation: Physical data is never encoded in the name.

options.text: The year the compound was first made
options.explanation: History plays no role in IUPAC names.

check.stem: What level of naming is expected of you in this specification?

options.text: Name simple straight-chain compounds and unbranched isomers with up to six carbons
options.explanation: The expectation covers straightforward chains and unbranched isomers within six carbons.

options.text: Generate any branched name from scratch, however complex
options.explanation: Branched names may appear in questions, but you are not usually asked to build them yourself.

options.text: Name only the first two members of each family
options.explanation: The ceiling is six carbons, not two; meth and eth are just the first stems.

options.text: Write trade names instead of systematic names
options.explanation: The specification expects IUPAC systematic names, not trade labels.

glossary.definition: The front part of an organic name, carrying the stem that counts the carbon atoms.
The end part of an organic name, identifying the functional group the compound carries.
The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, whose rules define compound names worldwide.
The name fragment that records the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.
The marker added before the second part of a name when two identical functional groups are present.

workedExample.prompt: a) Name the compound with a 3-carbon chain carrying an -OH group, explaining your construction. b) A molecule is named butene: how many carbon atoms has it and which functional group does it carry? c) Why are position numbers needed in propanol but not in ethanol?
steps: a) Propanol (propan-1-ol): the stem prop- counts 3 carbon atoms and the suffix -anol shows the alcohol (-OH) functional group.
b) The stem but- counts 4 carbon atoms and the suffix -ene shows a C=C double bond — butene is a 4-carbon alkene.

c) In propanol the -OH group could sit on more than one carbon, so the carbons are numbered and the name quotes the position (carbon 1); in ethanol there is only one carbon, so no position number is needed.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Propan-1-ol — prop- (3 carbons) + -anol (OH group). b) 4 carbon atoms, C=C. c) Position numbers locate the group when more than one position is possible.
